title: Design interfaces for posterity
concept: Prior to Java 8, it was impossible to add methods to an interface without breaking all existing implementations. Java 8 added default methods, but while default methods make it possible to add methods to existing interfaces, doing so is full of peril. A default method will be injected into all existing implementations without their knowledge or consent, and there is no guarantee that a generic default implementation will maintain the class invariants of all pre-existing implementations (e.g. synchronized collections or thread safety). Therefore, careful interface design before release remains paramount.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: Why is adding a default method to an existing interface risky?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: Because the default method may not satisfy the invariants of existing third-party implementations (e.g. breaking thread synchronization or failing with runtime exceptions).

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: What should you do before releasing a public interface to the world?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: Test it rigorously by creating at least three diverse, independent implementations to verify its design before it becomes frozen in stone.

quiz.question: What famous bug occurred in Apache Commons Collections when Java 8 introduced the `removeIf` default method to `java.util.Collection`?
options: Synchronized collection wrappers failed to synchronize on the lock during removeIf, causing race conditions and ConcurrentModificationExceptions
It caused a JVM OutOfMemoryError
It deleted all elements in the collection unconditionally
The compiler refused to load the bytecode

quiz.question: Does a default method compile into an interface if it conflicts with another default method from a second implemented interface?
options: No, the compiler emits an error requiring the implementing class to explicitly override and resolve the conflict
The JVM chooses whichever method was declared first alphabetically
The JVM picks the implementation from the larger interface
It compiles but throws an AbstractMethodError at runtime

quiz.question: What is the primary intended use case for default methods according to Effective Java?
options: To provide standard implementations of non-primitive methods when designing NEW interfaces, rather than casually modifying existing ones
To turn interfaces into concrete classes
To replace unit tests
To avoid creating class files

quiz.question: Can default methods be used to remove or rename existing methods in an interface?
options: No, default methods can only add new method implementations; they cannot delete or rename methods
Yes, by marking the old method with @DeprecatedDefault
Yes, in Java 11+
Only if the interface is package-private

quiz.question: Why is it virtually impossible to fix a fundamentally flawed public interface after release?
options: Changing or removing methods breaks binary and source compatibility for all external client applications
The JVM enforces digital signatures on all interfaces
Interfaces cannot be modified after compilation
Package managers reject updated interfaces

interview_questions.question: What does Joshua Bloch mean by 'design interfaces for posterity'?
interview_questions.model_answer: Once a public interface is released and adopted by external clients, modifying it without breaking existing code is nearly impossible. While Java 8 added default methods to reduce breakage, default methods can still corrupt class invariants at runtime. Therefore, interfaces must be designed with extreme care, foresight, and testing prior to release.

interview_questions.question: A library developer adds `default void audit() { ... }` to an interface implemented by security-sensitive classes. What risk does this create?
interview_questions.model_answer: Classes implementing the interface may assume that all methods are audited via a custom logging proxy or security wrapper. The newly injected default method bypasses those security wrappers unless third-party authors explicitly discover and override it.

interview_questions.question: What happens when a class inherits a concrete method from a superclass and a default method with the same signature from an interface?
interview_questions.model_answer: The 'Class Wins' rule applies: the superclass's method implementation always takes precedence over the interface's default method. Interface default methods are never chosen over concrete class implementations.

interview_questions.question: How should an API author test an interface before releasing it to production?
interview_questions.model_answer: Write at least three distinct, highly varied implementations of the interface (e.g. in-memory, file-backed, mock) and write multiple client applications that use the interface. This will immediately expose missing methods, awkward signatures, or over-constrained parameters before the API is set in stone.
